title: Working with Web APIs
intro: A **web API** is a web address that returns data, usually JSON, instead of a page. With the popular `requests` library you send a GET request, check the **status code** and read the JSON. Code here can't reach the internet, so these exercises use a practice copy of `requests` that answers for `https://api.example.com`. The code you write is the same as with the real library (`pip install requests`).

questions.prompt: Status `200` means OK; `4xx` means the request was wrong (404 = not found); `5xx` means the server failed. Always pass a `timeout` so a slow server can't freeze your program.
questions.exampleCode:
import requests

resp = requests.get("https://api.example.com/weather",
                    params={"city": "Oslo"}, timeout=5)
print(resp.status_code)      # 200
data = resp.json()           # JSON text -> Python dict
print(data["temp_c"], data["conditions"])
questions.explanation: `params` builds the `?city=Oslo` part of the address for you, escaping spaces and symbols.

questions.prompt: Get the weather for `Lisbon` from `https://api.example.com/weather` (pass the city in `params`, and a `timeout`). Store the temperature (the `temp_c` field) in `temp`.
questions.solution:
import requests

resp = requests.get("https://api.example.com/weather", params={"city": "Lisbon"}, timeout=5)
temp = resp.json()["temp_c"]

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert temp == 21, 'temp should be the temp_c value for Lisbon.'

tests.name: timeout
tests.code: assert requests.calls and requests.calls[-1]['timeout'], 'Pass a timeout to requests.get.'

questions.explanation: The JSON object becomes a Python dict, so you read fields with square brackets.

questions.prompt: An API answers with status code **404**. What does that mean?

options.text: The thing you asked for doesn't exist
You need to wait and retry

questions.hint: 4xx codes mean the request was the problem.
questions.explanation: 404 is *Not Found*. A crashed server sends 5xx; 200 means success.

questions.prompt: Write `get_temp(city)` that returns the city's `temp_c`, or `None` when the API answers 404 (unknown city).
questions.starterCode:
import requests

def get_temp(city):
    resp = requests.get("https://api.example.com/weather", params={"city": city}, timeout=5)
    return resp.json()["temp_c"]

tests.name: known
tests.code: assert get_temp('Oslo') == 4 and get_temp('Nairobi') == 25, 'Return temp_c for known cities.'

tests.name: unknown
tests.code: assert get_temp('Atlantis') is None, 'Unknown cities (404) should return None.'

questions.explanation: An error response still has a JSON body — just not the one you wanted. Check the status first.

questions.prompt: `json.loads` turns JSON text into Python values. What does this print?
questions.code:
import json

data = json.loads('{"items": [{"n": 1}, {"n": 2}], "next": null}')
print(sum(i["n"] for i in data["items"]), data["next"])
questions.explanation: Objects become dicts, arrays become lists, and `null` becomes `None` — exactly what `resp.json()` does too.

questions.prompt: This should list the names of active users from `https://api.example.com/users`, but crashes with *TypeError: 'Response' object is not iterable*. Fix it.
questions.starterCode:
import requests

users = requests.get("https://api.example.com/users", timeout=5)
active = [u["name"] for u in users if u["active"]]
questions.solution:
import requests

users = requests.get("https://api.example.com/users", timeout=5).json()
active = [u["name"] for u in users if u["active"]]

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert active == ['Ana', 'Caro', 'Dev'], 'active should be the names of the active users.'

questions.hint: `get` returns a response object, not the data.
questions.explanation: Call `.json()` to turn the response body into Python data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the argument name that sends `city=Oslo` as part of the request.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert resp.json()['city'] == 'Oslo', 'The response should be for Oslo.'

questions.hint: The query-string values are the request's *parameters*.

questions.prompt: `https://api.example.com/todos?page=1` returns `{"page": 1, "items": [...], "next": 2}`; the last page has `"next": null`. Write `fetch_all_todos()` that follows the pages and returns every item in one list. Pass a timeout on every request.
questions.solution:
import requests

def fetch_all_todos():
    items = []
    page = 1
    while page is not None:
        data = requests.get("https://api.example.com/todos", params={"page": page}, timeout=5).json()
        items.extend(data["items"])
        page = data["next"]
    return items

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert fetch_all_todos() == ['Buy milk', 'Call Ana', 'Book dentist', 'Pay rent', 'Water plants'], 'Return the items from every page, in order.'

tests.name: timeouts
tests.code:
requests.calls.clear()
fetch_all_todos()
assert len(requests.calls) == 3 and all(c['timeout'] for c in requests.calls), 'Make one request per page, each with a timeout.'
tests.message: One request per page, each with a timeout.

questions.hint: Loop while there's a next page: fetch it, add its items, move to `data["next"]`.
questions.explanation: Most APIs split long lists into pages. Following `next` until it's empty is the usual pattern.

questions.prompt: Write `fetch_json(url)` that returns the parsed JSON, but raises `requests.HTTPError` when the status is 4xx or 5xx.

tests.name: ok
tests.code: assert len(fetch_json('https://api.example.com/users')) == 4, 'Return the JSON for a successful request.'

tests.name: error
not found

questions.hint: `resp.raise_for_status()` does nothing for success and raises for errors.
questions.explanation: Failing loudly beats carrying on with an error message where you expected data.

options.text: Without it, a server that never answers can make your program wait forever

questions.hint: What happens if the server just never replies?
questions.explanation: `requests` waits indefinitely by default. A timeout turns a hang into an exception you can handle.

questions.prompt: Write `make_url(base, params)` that returns `base` plus a correctly escaped query string, using `urllib.parse.urlencode`.
questions.starterCode:
def make_url(base, params):
    return base + "?" + "&".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in params.items())

tests.name: escaped
tests.code: assert make_url('https://api.example.com/search', {'q': 'green tea & honey', 'page': 2}) == 'https://api.example.com/search?q=green+tea+%26+honey&page=2', 'Spaces and & must be escaped.'

questions.explanation: An unescaped `&` in a value would start a new parameter. That's why `params=` and `urlencode` exist.
